strengths: Fully end-to-end differentiable pipeline unifying multi-view 3D reconstruction (MVSplat-based inverse renderer), transformer-only particle dynamics, and Gaussian Splatting decoding, trained purely on an image reconstruction loss — a clean and coherent design that removes KNN graph construction and hand-crafted edge features.

Technically interesting extensions of PTv3 to temporally evolving point clouds: the temporally serialized point cloud (t-SPC) with batch codes, temporal encoding, and one-bit-shift temporal merging is a neat, reusable mechanism for spatio-temporal attention over point sets, and the ablations (Table S6) show the design choices matter.

Comprehensive ablation studies (rollout length, camera setup, segmentation masks, modality configuration, grid resolution, temporal merging) that give genuine insight, e.g., the latent-vs-explicit representation robustness to reduced camera counts (Table S2) and the camera-specific overfitting failure mode of explicit representations.

Honest limitations discussion: reliance on multi-view data, lack of real-world validation, no explicit occlusion handling, and acknowledgment that baselines are hard to compare; the paper also commits to open-source release of code and datasets, which addresses the reproducibility gap left by prior works (VPD, HD-VPD, DEL, 3D-IntPhys).

Interesting qualitative demonstrations of emergent capabilities: scene editing, generalization to multi-body interactions from single-object training, and shadow modeling, suggesting the learned representation captures more than surface-level dynamics.
weaknesses: Evaluation is entirely on synthetic, self-introduced datasets with only 6 objects per dataset and a single interaction scenario per dataset (falling on a ground plane, falling on a cloth). The central claim of learning 'real world physics' and generalizable simulators is not tested on any real-world data, and the authors concede validation on real datasets is left to future work.

The main quantitative evidence is image-space PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS on held-out trajectories. There is no physics-level evaluation (e.g., trajectory error, contact accuracy, deformation metrics), so it is hard to judge whether the model truly learns dynamics or exploits photometric shortcuts; the claimed 'physically plausible' behavior in scene-editing and multi-body experiments is assessed only qualitatively.

The baseline comparison is weak and not apples-to-apples: the only quantitative comparison is against Cosmos, a large pretrained video generation model with language conditioning, evaluated with hand-written text prompts. No particle-based simulator baseline is actually run, and the claimed advantages over GNN-based PBS methods (VPD, HD-VPD, etc.) are argued from Table 1 design properties rather than measured results.

Generalization claims (unseen multibody interactions, novel scene edits, shadow reasoning) rest on cherry-picked qualitative examples and supplementary figures; error accumulation over long rollouts (Fig. 8 shows PSNR degrading substantially within ~20 future steps) suggests limited long-horizon stability, and 'near real-time' speeds of 16-42 FPS on an H100 are modest relative to the framing.

Several components are adopted rather than invented (MVSplat, 3DGS, PTv3, FiLM conditioning); the novelty lies mainly in the temporal serialization/merging scheme and the joint training recipe, which is a solid but incremental system contribution. Ablations are also restricted to a single dataset (elastic), limiting evidence that the design choices transfer across dynamics regimes.

Reproducibility details for training are given (seeds, steps, hardware), but the datasets are new and results rely on ~12% held-out splits with large variance bands (e.g., ±3-5 dB PSNR); independent verification will depend entirely on the promised code/data release.

strengths: Technically coherent end-to-end pipeline: the paper clearly unifies inverse rendering (MVSplat + FiLM-based view-independent feature unprojection), a transformer dynamics model over temporally serialized point clouds (extending PTv3 with t-SPC codes and temporal merging), and Gaussian splatting decoding, all trained with an image reconstruction loss.

The temporal merging / serialization mechanism (Eq. 5-7) is a clean and well-motivated extension of PTv3 to time-varying point clouds, and the ablations in Appendix B (rollout length, camera setup, segmentation masks, modality, grid resolution, temporal merger) are thorough and honestly reported.

Honest limitations section acknowledging multi-view data requirements, occlusion handling, and that validation is synthetic-only/proof-of-concept; open-source code and dataset release is promised and improves reproducibility relative to closely related works (VPD, HD-VPD, DEL) that have no public code.

Demonstrated qualitative capabilities beyond training distribution (scene editing, multi-object duplication, shadow reasoning) are interesting evidence that removing hand-crafted graph biases does not destroy generalization.
weaknesses: Lack of any quantitative comparison to a particle-based learned simulator baseline. Table 1 motivates the work against VPD, HD-VPD, DEL, 3D-IntPhys, etc., but the only quantitative comparison is against Cosmos, a general video generation foundation model that is arguably mismatched to this task and not directly comparable (the authors concede this). Reimplementing at least one particle-based baseline, or evaluating on a benchmark those methods used, would substantially strengthen the central claim that 'minimal-bias' transformer dynamics outperform GNN-based alternatives.

The core claim that removing GNN inductive biases improves dynamics is supported mainly by qualitative results and comparisons against an ill-matched baseline; there is no controlled ablation of GNN vs. transformer dynamics within the same framework.

Evaluation is entirely on synthetic, self-collected datasets with PSNR/SSIM/LIPS as metrics. Rendered-image metrics are an indirect proxy for physical fidelity, and no quantitative physical accuracy (e.g., trajectory error against simulator state) is reported, making it hard to verify claims about physically plausible dynamics and generalization.

All training data is simulated with simple scenarios (single object on a ground plane, fixed cloth corners); the multi-object generalization claims rest on a handful of qualitative figures rather than systematic quantitative evaluation.

The spatial serialization bit budget and hyperparameters (e.g., grid size 0.004 m spanning '216 m per axis', 48-bit spatial codes) suggest tight scene-scale coupling; robustness to scene scale is asserted but not clearly demonstrated.
Significance is currently that of a proof-of-concept/baseline release rather than a demonstrated advance over state of the art; this is legitimate but limits the reach of the contribution.

strengths: The paper presents a fully end-to-end differentiable framework that unifies inverse rendering (MVSplat-based encoder with a FiLM-conditioned view-independent feature transformation), a transformer-only particle dynamics model (PTv3 extended with temporal serialization, encoding, and merging), and Gaussian-splatting-based decoding, trained purely on an image reconstruction loss — a coherent and well-motivated system design.

The extension of PTv3 to temporally evolving point clouds (t-SPC serialization keys with temporal merging, Eq. 5–7) is a technically interesting and reusable contribution that reuses the same attention block across time steps rather than per-timestep modules.

Demonstrated generalization is compelling for a learned simulator: multi-body scenes not seen in training, scene edits (ground removal, altered geometry), and apparent shadow modeling (Fig. 9), supported by an extensive appendix with ablations on rollout length, camera setup, grid resolution, temporal merging, and segmentation masks.

Strong reproducibility commitment: the authors promise open-source code and datasets, provide detailed hyperparameters and training costs (single H100, ~5 days), and honestly document that prior baselines (VPD, HD-VPD, DEL, 3D-IntPhys) lack public code/data — an honest treatment of why direct comparison is infeasible.
Honest limitations section: reliance on multi-view data, occlusion handling, and restriction to synthetic validation are clearly acknowledged rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The evaluation is limited to self-collected synthetic datasets with no real-world validation, weakening the central claim of learning 'real world physics directly from video data'. The paper frames itself as a proof of concept, but the abstract's claims about capturing 'diverse physical behaviors' rest on three simulated datasets with simple ground-plane interactions.

The baseline comparison is weak. The only quantitative comparison is against Cosmos (a pretrained video generation model), which the authors themselves note is 'not directly comparable' and is prompt-conditioned with no 3D grounding. No particle-based simulator baseline (e.g., a reimplementation of VPD or a GNN variant) is evaluated, so it is unclear whether the transformer/SFC design choices actually outperform simpler GNN alternatives — the core 'remove inductive bias' thesis is not tested against the biased baselines it criticizes.

Evaluation relies exclusively on image-space metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS). There is no quantitative measure of physical fidelity (e.g., trajectory error, penetration depth, energy conservation), so claims about physical plausibility, rigid-body integrity in multi-body scenes, and shadow reasoning are supported mainly by qualitative figures.

Several claims are under-supported: '3DGSim is currently the only open-source, particle-based simulator trained directly on videos' is asserted without rigorous verification; the shadow-learning observation (Fig. 9) could plausibly be an artifact of appearance supervision rather than scene understanding, and no controlled experiment is provided.

Some experiments show degradation over long rollouts (Fig. 8 shows declining PSNR and increasing variance), and error bars are large relative to some reported differences (e.g., 3DGSim variants in Table 11 overlap within ±2 dB), making some conclusions less robust than presented.

Datasets are modest in scale and diversity (six objects per dataset, single interaction type each: falling onto a plane or fixed cloth), which limits the evidence for the claimed diversity of 'rigid, elastic, cloth-like dynamics, and boundary conditions'.

strengths: End-to-end differentiable pipeline (MVSplat-style inverse renderer -> PTv3-based dynamics -> 3DGS decoding) trained purely from multi-view RGB with image reconstruction loss is a clean and well-motivated instantiation of the 'learned particle simulator from raw video' direction, and the paper clearly articulates how it differs from GNN-based PBS (no kNN graphs, no hand-crafted edge features) and from physics-prior methods like PhysGaussian/PhysDreamer (Appendix D.2 is a thorough, honest comparison).

The temporal encoding/merging (TEM) extension of PTv3 to temporally evolving point clouds is a genuinely neat technical contribution: the bit-shift merging of serialization codes is simple, memory-efficient, and allows one attention block to be reused across timesteps, unlike Whitney et al. (2024). The ablations (Tab. 1, Tables S3-S8) are extensive and convincingly show TEM is critical (-14.96 dB without it) and that latent > explicit representations matters, especially with fewer cameras (Table S4).

The paper goes beyond in-distribution evaluation: OOD scene edits (ground removal, raised drop heights, duplicated/multi-object scenes), emergent behaviors (shadows, weight-induced penetration), and preliminary real-world results on HO-Cap with a pretrained DepthAnything3 encoder and 120-step rollouts. Honest reporting of failure modes (Fig. S15) is commendable.

Reproducibility: the authors commit to releasing code and dataset, provide detailed architectures, training hyperparameters, FPS/VRAM figures (Appendix A.4), and careful justification for image-based evaluation metrics (Appendix E).
weaknesses: The baseline coverage is thin relative to the claims. The strongest related 3D learned simulators (VPD, HD-VPD, DEL, 3D-IntPhys) are not compared at all, justified by unavailability of code/data; the main quantitative comparison is against Cosmos (a 2D video model), and Spring-Gaus is acknowledged to be an unfair comparison (needs GT constraints, per-trajectory optimization, cannot handle cloth/collisions). The 'state-of-the-art' framing therefore rests mostly on beating a differently-conditioned 2D baseline, which weakens the evidential support for the central superiority claim.

Evaluation is confined to small-scale synthetic data: three datasets with only 6 objects each (~1000 + 2x200 trajectories), and the test split is held-out trajectories of the same objects rather than held-out objects. Cross-object/multi-body generalization is shown only qualitatively (Figs. 10, S6-S9). The real-world experiment is preliminary, action-conditioned, qualitative-only, and swaps the encoder, so the RGB-only 'scales to data-rich regimes' narrative is not yet empirically demonstrated.

Claims of 'physically plausible', 'learns generalized physical laws', and 'holistic understanding of lighting, geometry, and physics' are supported only by qualitative visuals and image-space metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/FVD). There are no dynamics-specific quantitative measures (e.g., trajectory error after registration, contact-time or energy consistency checks), and the Appendix E justification, while reasonable, does not substitute for at least one physics-grounded metric on the synthetic data where GT dynamics are available.

Several presentation issues undermine polish: the Discussion contains a garbled sentence ('future work will further explore action conditioningto enable large-scale validation... for passive phenomena'), the Genesis citation is 'Authors, G.', Figure 2's caption claims 'training on less than 6 minutes of video per object across 6 objects' while the rigid dataset is separately described, inconsistent grid-resolution tables (0.0012 in Table S7), and the notable-but-unexplained result that 2-12 latent achieves better FVD than 4-12 latent is glossed over.

Scalability and efficiency claims are partly borrowed: the argument that kNN costs 54% of forward time cites another paper rather than measuring a GNN baseline on this task, and the 6-day single-H100 training time with small datasets leaves the 'scalable computation over hand-crafted biases' thesis largely unproven at scale.

Novelty is compositional: MVSplat, PTv3, 3DGS, FiLM conditioning are all existing components; the genuinely new pieces (view-independent FiLM feature unprojection, temporal merging of serialized codes, invariant/dynamic feature decomposition) are incremental engineering advances, albeit well-executed and validated.

strengths: The core question — whether graph-based inductive biases can be dropped in favor of a transformer-only dynamics engine trained purely from multi-view RGB — is well motivated and represents a sensible, coherent system-level contribution by combining MVSplat, a PTv3-style spatiotemporal transformer with a novel temporal-merging mechanism, and 3DGS decoding.

The temporal encoding and merging (TEM) extension of PTv3 is a concrete technical idea that plausibly enables multi-timestep conditioning within a single attention model; the ablations (Tab. 1, Tab. S3–S8) are extensive and support the importance of rollout length, temporal merging timing, and the latent representation.

The paper is refreshingly honest about limitations: the discussion of the 2D-vs-3D tradeoff (Sec. 6), the failure-case analysis (Fig. S15), the variable-length input degradation (Tab. S2), and the camera-count sensitivity (Tab. S4) are candid and useful for future work.
A code and dataset release is promised, which improves reproducibility relative to the baselines the authors criticize (VPD, HD-VPD, DEL, 3D-IntPhys release neither code nor data).
Preliminary real-world experiments on HO-Cap show effort to move beyond synthetic data.
weaknesses: The central claims of physical plausibility and out-of-distribution generalization (ground removal, multi-object interactions, emergent shadows) are supported almost entirely by cherry-picked qualitative figures. There is no quantitative OOD evaluation, no object-tracking or deformation-error metric, and no statistical comparison of 3DGSim vs. CosmosFT on the generalization scenarios that headline the abstract and Sec. 5.3.

The evaluation is exclusively image-space (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/FVD). Section E argues that particle-level metrics conflate reconstruction with dynamics, but this justification is not fully convincing; without any dynamics-specific quantitative measure, the claim that the model has 'learned physics' rather than short-horizon appearance extrapolation is under-supported. The gap between the 12-step training rollout and the claimed 80-step (Fig. 8) and 120-step (HO-Cap) rollouts is not quantitatively bridged.

The baseline comparison is weak. The most relevant learned 3D particle simulators (VPD, HD-VPD, DEL, 3D-IntPhys) are excluded, and the sole 3D baseline (Spring-Gaus) is itself acknowledged by the authors to be an unfair comparison (requires GT constraints, same-trajectory optimization, no cloth/multi-body support). Against this weak field, 'competitive with state-of-the-art' claims overstate the evidence.

The synthetic datasets are very small and narrow: six objects per dataset, trained on minutes of footage, with a single collision type (object vs. circular ground plane). It is unclear how much of the apparent generalization reflects memorization of a single simple contact pattern. Ablations are additionally run only on the elastic dataset.

The real-world results rely on action conditioning via sparse 3D hand keypoints — a privileged signal — and on a pretrained DepthAnything3 backbone, which sits uneasily with the paper's motivating narrative of avoiding privileged signals, and makes the HO-Cap results non-comparable to the synthetic setup. The quantitative analysis offered is only against a 'constant frame' baseline, which is a very low bar.

Several quantitative claims lack supporting evidence: the '1–2 orders of magnitude faster to train and simulate' claim in Sec. D.2 has no timing table; the widely quoted '54% of forward time' for kNN is cited from another work's setting.

There are presentation defects that undermine polish and accuracy: a broken sentence in the Discussion ('further explore action conditioningto enable large-scale validation ... for passive phenomena'), Table S7 lists a grid resolution (0.0012) that contradicts the stated tested set, Figure 2's 'less than 6 minutes of video per object across 6 objects' leaves the train/test protocol ambiguous, and the ablation text in C.2 reports PSNR 33.15 for a different setup than the main model without explanation.

At ~6 days on an H100 for six objects, the scalability story is asserted but not demonstrated at scale; the paper does not include any experiment that stresses the claimed efficiency advantage over GNN-based simulators.

strengths: Novel and significant contribution: 3DGSim is, to my knowledge, the first fully end-to-end differentiable 3D particle-based simulator trained purely from multi-view RGB videos (no depth, GT particles, or physics priors), combining MVSplat-based inverse rendering, a transformer-only dynamics engine built on PTv3, and Gaussian Splatting decoding under a single image reconstruction loss. This directly addresses the stated gap in the PBS literature (Whitney et al., Wang et al., etc.).

Technical substance beyond assembly: the Temporal Encoding & Merging (TEM) extension of PTv3 to temporally serialized point clouds is a non-trivial architectural contribution, and the view-independent inverse renderer (FiLM conditioning on depth, pixel shift, Plücker rays) is a sensible solution to the camera-bound-feature problem in MVSplat.

Unusually thorough ablation suite: Table 1 plus supplementary Sections B, C.1-C.6 cover rollout length, input windows, latent vs. explicit representations, camera setups, segmentation masks, grid resolution, and temporal merger strides. The finding that TEM removal collapses performance (~18 PSNR) and that explicit 3DGS representations overfit to camera viewpoints (C.2) directly substantiates the paper's central 'give up graph inductive bias' claim.

Beyond in-distribution evaluation: the OOD scene-editing experiments (ground removal, object duplication, multi-body interactions, emergent shadows) and the preliminary real-world results on HO-Cap with 120-step rollouts are compelling evidence that the model learns transferable dynamics rather than memorizing trajectories. The failure-mode analysis (Fig. S15) is honest and insightful.

Strong reproducibility: open-source code and dataset release, detailed hyperparameters, training cost disclosure (single H100, ~6 days), and FPS/VRAM reporting. Baseline limitations are candidly explained (VPD/DEL/3D-IntPhys code unavailable; Spring-Gaus caveats discussed in detail in B.1 and D.2).

Honest limitations discussion: the Discussion section explicitly acknowledges the multi-view dependency, occlusion modeling gaps, and the particle creation/destruction tradeoff versus 2D generative models. Sec. E provides a reasonable rationale for why image-space metrics are used instead of GT particle-state metrics.
weaknesses: Dynamics accuracy is never quantified against physical ground truth. All quantitative results are image-space metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/FVD). While Sec. E gives a defensible rationale (non-unique reconstruction), this means central claims like 'physically plausible' and 'accurately predicts motion' rest on qualitative visual inspection and inference from emergent behaviors (shadows, freefall under ground removal). A quantitative physics evaluation (e.g., Chamfer distance after registration, or GT-state evaluation as an oracle upper bound) would materially strengthen the work.

Baseline comparisons are weak in the 3D regime. The main comparable learned PBS baselines (VPD, HD-VPD, DEL, 3D-IntPhys) were neither run nor reimplemented; the only 3D comparison (Spring-Gaus) is acknowledged by the authors as unfair for multiple reasons. The Cosmos comparison is against a 2D video model, which the paper itself argues is not the right comparison class for its core claims. Consequently, it is difficult to establish how much of the performance derives from the proposed design versus the general capability of modern components.

Scale and diversity of training data are modest: three synthetic datasets of only 6 objects each, single-body ground collisions, single ground geometry. OOD results (multi-object, ground removal) are shown for few scenes and only qualitatively, so generalization claims, while promising, rest on limited evidence.

The real-world results require a substantial system change (MVSplat replaced by DepthAnything3, sparse hand keypoints as action conditioning, context-camera-only reconstruction loss) and are trained on only 64 trajectories; they are appropriately labeled 'preliminary' but are not directly comparable to the synthetic evaluation setup.

Some presentation issues: Figure 8's per-dataset interpretation is thin (e.g., FVD in Table S1 sometimes favors the 2-step variant over the 4-step 'final' model, which is not discussed); minor typos ('action conditioningto', 'for out scene size', 'unnable'); the abstract claims of 'realistic lighting effects' rest on a single shadow example (Fig. 11).

The claim that the transformer-only design avoids expensive kNN computation (54% of forward time cited from Wu et al.) is asserted but never measured in 3DGSim itself; no runtime comparison against a GNN-based variant is provided, so the efficiency argument for dropping graph bias is only indirect (via TEM ablation accuracy, not speed).
